doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Joe Williams and meeting Jo Jones
summary: At Randall's Island, his mother's remark leads Jo Jones to adopt Phil as a babysitter.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: Let me run a couple of names by you. Joe Williams?

Well he was the reason why I met Jo Jones. When we were at the Randall’s Island Festival in 1956 and Count Basie band was plenty hot and they had “Everyday I Have the Blues” which was a hit single, and the album “April in Paris,” which I believe had come out as a big selling record, and my mother and I got backstage, and she was like holding my hand and this man started talking to her. In retrospect I now realize that he was probably hitting on my mother, and he said, “Well this is all very well and good we are backstage hearing Count Basie but if you play your cards right I can get you further backstage and you could actually meet Joe Williams.” So my mother completely pops his balloon and says, “Well that’s all very well and good but of course Jimmy Rushing was the only singer for the Count Basie Orchestra.” Poof — he disappears. Jo Jones taps my mother from behind on the shoulder and says, “Madam I heard that, that was wonderful, you seem to know about our orchestra.” “Not as much as my little boy here.” “Okay

mister.” I was five. It would be another fifteen years before anyone would ever call me mister again. “Okay mister, who’s Prince Robinson?” “The tenor player in McKinney’s Cottonpickers.” I didn’t have that voice. “The tenor player with McKinney’s Cottonpickers.” And Jo Jones announced to my mother that she had acquired a new babysitter. That was the breakthrough. So Joe Williams doesn’t have too much to do in that story but he’s the triggering mechanism.
